column1: # Model scope: which production functions are bound to a TLA+ spec.
# Columns are tab-separated:
#   <func>\t<file>\t<spec>\t<state-cover fixture>
# scripts/ci/check-model-scope.sh reads this and, for a change that touches one
# of these functions, asks that the spec and its fixture move too. It proves
# nothing -- it turns "the model quietly stopped tracking the code" into a
# review prompt. A change that legitimately does not affect the model passes by
# saying so: put `Model-scope-ok: <reason>` in a commit message or the PR body.
# What is NOT here matters as much as what is. No state-cover fixture binds
# these machines to their code, so `make formal-verify` says nothing about them.
# The first has a spec and no Go binding; the rest have no spec at all:
#   * the wake agent's hold path (internal/wakeagent: demandTracker,
#     readinessTracker) -- MODELLED by formal/WakeAgentHold.tla but not bound to
#     Go, and deliberately so rather than by omission: the state it holds is
#     unexported in-memory bookkeeping in a package that must not import the
#     controller (or controller-runtime) at all, so there is no materialisable
#     state for a state-cover harness to project. Its two invariants
#     (Inv_NoStrandedWaiter, Inv_WaiterRefsAccurate) are therefore checked by
#     TLC only; internal/wakeagent's own unit tests are what hold a line under
#     the Go side. Binding it needs an exported test seam on the tracker, which
#     is a decision about that package's API rather than a gap in this table
#   * FireboltEngineClass merge / drift detection (stsMatchesSpec and the
#     effective* resolvers)
#   * drain probing and its timeouts (deliberately deferred: fuzzed time is the
#     highest false-positive axis)
# So "the TLA+ suite passes" means "the modelled machines still agree with their
# specs", not "this change is verified". Adding a machine here means writing a
# spec for it; SigningKeyRotation.tla is the smallest worked example,
# counterexample config included.
